strengths: Develops a technically rigorous dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for linear/kernel regression with power-law eigenvalue spectra, using MSRDJ formalism and variational Gaussian approximation, with detailed appendix derivations that aid reproducibility.

Successfully unifies several previously disparate frameworks (Bayesian GP inference, deterministic gradient flow with/without weight decay, and stochastic Langevin dynamics) as special cases of a single formalism, clarifying their relationships.

The resulting theory yields an interpretable, low-dimensional description (via order parameters: response function, correlation functions) of high-dimensional training dynamics, decoupling into per-mode equations coupled only through collective quantities.

Simulations (Figs. 1-4) show good quantitative agreement between theoretical predictions and numerical experiments across a range of noise levels and regularization strengths, supporting the correctness of the derivation.

The bias-variance decomposition of the dynamic generalization error provides a clear, mechanistic explanation for the empirically known benefit of early stopping under noisy training, and clarifies how regularization interacts with the variance-driven divergence at late times.
Clear related-work section carefully differentiating the contribution from prior work (Krogh & Hertz, Advani et al., Canatar et al., Bordelon et al.), situating the theoretical advance appropriately.
weaknesses: Despite the title's emphasis on 'neural scaling laws,' the paper does not present the canonical scaling-law evidence (e.g., log-log plots of test loss vs. dataset size P or model size N showing power-law decay); all empirical figures instead show test error as a function of training time t. The connection to scaling laws in the classical sense is asserted but not directly visualized or quantified.

The theory and all experiments are restricted to linear/kernel (NNGP-limit) regression with synthetic Gaussian features and idealized power-law spectra; no validation on real data or real (even lazy-trained) neural networks is provided, limiting evidence for claimed relevance to practical networks.

The comparison to the closest related work (Bordelon et al., 2025) is only qualitative (claiming 'fewer and more interpretable order parameters') without a concrete quantitative or empirical comparison demonstrating this advantage.

The core qualitative finding—that early stopping is beneficial due to a bias-variance trade-off in noisy training—is largely consistent with prior results (e.g., Advani et al., 2020); the paper's novelty lies mainly in extending this analysis to power-law spectra and stochastic dynamics, which is a more incremental than transformative contribution.

The dense, notation-heavy presentation (especially the extensive appendix derivations) may hinder accessibility; the main text would benefit from more intuitive exposition of what the order parameters mean physically and why the specific approximations (Gaussian VGA, Wishart disorder average) are justified in this setting.

Key modeling assumptions (i.i.d. Gaussian features, orthogonality of feature dimensions, teacher-student setup) are common simplifications but their fidelity to real high-dimensional data with power-law spectra is not discussed as a limitation, nor is sensitivity to violations of these assumptions explored.

strengths: The MSRDJ/dynamical mean-field theory derivation is methodologically careful and the appendix provides a complete, self-contained derivation of the variational Gaussian approximation, the order parameters (R, C, C̃), and the resulting effective single-mode stochastic equations, which is a genuine technical contribution to the statistical-physics toolkit for learning theory.

The framework nicely unifies several previously disparate treatments (Bayesian GP inference, gradient flow with/without weight decay, Langevin SGD) under one set of order parameters and shows how a single memory kernel K and effective colored noise govern all of them, which is conceptually elegant.

The related-work section is thorough and carefully delineates the paper's position relative to closely related prior work (Krogh & Hertz, Advani et al., Canatar et al., Maloney et al., Bordelon et al.), correctly identifying what is and is not covered by each.

The theory-simulation agreement shown in Figures 1-4 is good for the toy setting considered, providing some validation of the derived equations of motion and the resulting bias-variance decomposition of the test error.
weaknesses: The central advertised contribution—an analytical account of 'neural scaling laws' as a function of the power-law exponent γ—is not actually demonstrated. No figure or derivation in the main text shows the scaling of the (stationary or early-stopped) generalization error as a function of dataset size P or network width N for varying γ, which is the standard definition of a 'neural scaling law' in the literature the paper claims to explain (e.g., Kaplan et al., Maloney et al., Bordelon et al.). Only time-dynamics at fixed, single γ=3/2 and fixed small P=N=100 are shown.

The bullet-point claim that the paper 'obtains analytical results that relate the power-law exponent of the feature kernel, regularization, and early stopping time to obtain a minimal generalization gap' is not substantiated with an explicit closed-form result or a systematic sweep over γ; the discussion of early stopping and regularization effects (Section 4.3) is qualitative/heuristic rather than quantitative on this specific relationship.

All experiments are confined to a small synthetic toy setting (N=P=100, Gaussian i.i.d. features with imposed power-law variance, fixed exponent), with no connection to real data, real network architectures, or even moderately large-scale simulations. This severely limits the evidence that the theory actually explains empirically observed neural scaling laws in practice, despite the title and abstract's strong framing around this phenomenon.

The qualitative phenomena highlighted (early stopping helps under noise, regularization bounds variance) are already established in prior cited work (Advani et al. 2020; Canatar et al. 2021; Krogh & Hertz), and the paper does not clearly quantify what new, falsifiable, or practically useful prediction follows from the added generality (time-dependent stochastic dynamics with power-law spectra) beyond reproducing known qualitative trends.

The comparison with the most closely related work (Bordelon et al. 2025) is asserted rather than demonstrated — the claim of 'fewer and more interpretable order parameters' is not backed by a side-by-side derivation, complexity comparison, or numerical comparison of predictions.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy even in the main text (e.g., Eqs. 19-30 involve multiple nested convolution operators and un-interpreted objects like K, R̄, C̄ introduced in rapid succession), with limited intuitive exposition bridging the physics formalism to ML-relevant takeaways for a non-specialist ICML audience.

No code, data, or implementation details (e.g., how the Volterra/convolution equations are numerically solved, time-stepping scheme beyond dt values) are provided in the main text, raising reproducibility concerns for the self-consistent numerical solution of the DMFT equations.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely unifying theoretical framework (via MSRDJ/dynamical mean-field theory) that subsumes Bayesian GP regression, gradient flow with/without weight decay, and Langevin training dynamics as special cases of a single formalism, which is a conceptually valuable synthesis of previously disparate threads in the literature (Krogh & Hertz, Advani et al., Canatar et al., Bordelon et al.).

The derivation is carried out carefully and rigorously using tools from disordered-systems field theory (disorder averaging over Wishart-distributed feature kernels, variational Gaussian approximation), with the full technical derivation documented in extensive appendices, supporting reproducibility of the theoretical results.

The resulting theory decouples the dynamics into statistically independent eigenmodes coupled only through a self-consistent response function and effective noise statistics, yielding an interpretable low-dimensional order-parameter description; the authors note this requires fewer order parameters than closely related prior work (Bordelon et al., 2024).

Theoretical predictions (mean discrepancy decay, test error dynamics, bias-variance decomposition, effects of regularization and noise) are directly compared against numerical simulations in Figures 1-4, and the agreement is generally good across a range of noise and regularization strengths, lending empirical support to the derived equations.

The bias-variance decomposition offers a mechanistic, quantitative explanation for the practical heuristic of early stopping and clarifies the interplay between regularization strength and noise-driven variance growth, which is a useful qualitative insight consistent with intuition and prior empirical observations.
weaknesses: All empirical validation is restricted to small synthetic systems (N=P=100) with a single power-law exponent (γ=1/2, i.e., Λ_ii ~ i^{-3/2}) and idealized Gaussian random features; there is no experiment on real data, real/trained neural network kernels, or a systematic sweep over the power-law exponent γ, data size P, or dimension N to explicitly verify the claimed link to 'neural scaling laws' (power-law exponents of generalization error vs. P/N), despite this being a central motivating claim of the paper and title.

The work is confined to the linear/NNGP (lazy) regime, explicitly excluding feature learning; while the authors acknowledge this limitation, the practical relevance of the theory to real-world large-model scaling laws (the primary motivation in the introduction) is not demonstrated, leaving a gap between the motivating narrative and the delivered scope.

The claimed advantage of using 'fewer and more interpretable order parameters' compared to Bordelon et al. (2024/2025) is stated qualitatively but not substantiated with a direct quantitative or side-by-side comparison, making it hard to assess the practical significance of the methodological improvement.

The paper is very dense and notation-heavy (e.g., overlines/bars for teacher weights, Λ vs η used interchangeably across main text and figures, inconsistent indexing conventions), which may hinder accessibility and reproducibility for readers outside the specific statistical-field-theory community; some symbols (e.g., Λ_ij in figures vs η_i in text) are not clearly reconciled.

No code or implementation details (e.g., numerical integration scheme validation, convergence checks for the self-consistent equations) are provided beyond stating time-step values, which limits practical reproducibility despite the thorough analytical appendix.

The significance of the contribution relative to closely related concurrent work (Bordelon et al. 2025, Canatar et al. 2021) is somewhat incremental: the core techniques (MSRDJ, disorder averaging, variational Gaussian approximation) are standard in the statistical-physics-of-learning literature, and the main novelty is the specific combination and simplification rather than a fundamentally new phenomenon or method.

strengths: Develops a rigorous dynamical mean-field theory (via MSRDJ formalism and variational Gaussian approximation) for stochastic Langevin training of random feature/kernel regression with power-law eigenvalue spectra, providing a principled unification of Bayesian GP inference, gradient flow (with/without weight decay), and Langevin dynamics as special cases of one framework.

The theory yields interpretable, low-dimensional order parameters (response function, correlation function) governing the full high-dimensional dynamics, and the derivation carefully tracks which diagrammatic/disorder terms survive in the large-N limit, with an extensive appendix providing a mostly self-contained derivation.

Recovers established results as limiting cases (the stationary result of Canatar et al. 2021 in the noiseless t→∞ limit, and the N→∞ compute-optimal scaling of Bordelon et al. 2024), which serves as a useful sanity check on the theory's correctness.

The bias-variance decomposition of the dynamical generalization error gives a clean, testable explanation for early stopping, including an explicit, empirically-validated formula for optimal stopping time as a function of inverse temperature alone, and additional scaling-law expressions relating power-law exponent, regularization, and data/parameter count.

Simulations across several parameter settings (varying noise, regularization, sample size) show good quantitative agreement between theory and simulation, and extensions to label noise and (briefly) nonlinear committee machines are sketched, indicating the framework's potential generality.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is entirely synthetic (teacher-student Gaussian features with an imposed power-law kernel spectrum, small system sizes N=P~100-1000); there is no experiment connecting the theory to actual trained neural networks or real data, which weakens the paper's motivating claim about explaining scaling laws observed in practice.

The theory is restricted to linear/kernel regression (NNGP/NTK/random-feature limits) and explicitly does not capture feature learning; the extension to nonlinear committee machines is only sketched in an appendix as future work rather than developed or validated.

Key structural assumptions (i.i.d. Gaussian features, orthogonality condition, exact power-law spectrum) are strong idealizations, and the self-averaging property central to the disorder-averaging argument is asserted with a heuristic justification rather than a rigorous proof.

The technical machinery (MSRDJ/statistical field theory for disordered systems applied to kernel regression dynamics) closely follows prior work (e.g., Bordelon et al. 2024, Helias & Dahmen 2020); while the paper argues for fewer/more interpretable order parameters and added L2-regularization treatment, the incremental novelty relative to this closely related dynamical literature could be more sharply delineated.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, with the core derivations relegated to a very long appendix; some inconsistencies/typos appear in the appendix (e.g., index and superscript errors), and reproducibility details (e.g., how the self-consistent Volterra-type equations are numerically solved, code availability) are not clearly discussed.

Limitations are only briefly discussed at the end of the paper (restriction to linearized settings), without deeper discussion of the practical impact of the idealized assumptions or computational cost of the self-consistent theory.

strengths: The paper employs a sophisticated and largely self-consistent dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) framework (MSRDJ formalism, disorder-averaging over Wishart-distributed feature kernels, variational Gaussian approximation) to unify several previously separate strands of the literature: static Bayesian/kernel-regression results (Canatar et al. 2021), gradient-flow dynamics with power-law data (Bordelon et al. 2024), and Langevin/stochastic training with weight decay.

The theory yields a compact reduction of the high-dimensional dynamics to two self-averaging order parameters (response function and autocorrelation), and the authors explicitly demonstrate internal consistency by recovering the stationary-state results of Canatar et al. (2021) as a t→∞ special case (Section I), lending credibility to the derivation.

Reasonably careful numerical experiments (bias-variance decomposition, effect of regularization, optimal early-stopping time vs. β) are provided and match the theoretical predictions closely across several parameter regimes (Figs. 1–5), providing empirical support for the analytic claims.

The derived closed-form scaling laws for bias, variance, and the optimal early-stopping time (e.g., t* = βα/(2(1+α))) are interpretable and offer testable, falsifiable predictions connecting spectral exponent, regularization, and noise level.

Extensions to label noise (Appendix H) and a preliminary (though undeveloped) generalization to nonlinear committee machines (Appendix J) suggest the framework has some flexibility beyond the core linear setting.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is incremental relative to closely related prior work (Bordelon et al. 2024, Canatar et al. 2021, Paquette et al.): it largely re-derives known bias-variance/early-stopping phenomenology for power-law kernel regression using a different (field-theoretic) technique, and the claim of being "more compact and interpretable" than Bordelon et al. is asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated (no direct quantitative or computational comparison of the two formalisms is given).

The setup assumes identical student and teacher features (rather than the down-projected/feature-learning student-teacher setups used in the closest related dynamical works), which narrows the phenomena the theory can capture and removes exactly the feature-learning effects that much of the current scaling-law literature is most interested in.

All empirical validation is on synthetic Gaussian random-feature/power-law-eigenvalue data with small, fixed system sizes (mostly N=P=100); there is no evaluation on real data, real kernels (e.g., NTK/NNGP of actual architectures), or larger-scale settings, which limits confidence that the predicted power laws are practically relevant beyond the idealized theoretical construction.

Central claims about self-averaging and the exactness of the variational Gaussian approximation in the N→∞ limit rely on informal diagrammatic/cumulant counting arguments (Appendix C) rather than a rigorous proof, which is standard in the statistical-physics literature but weakens the rigor of the "exactness" claim made in the discussion.

The presentation is dense, with most of the technical substance relegated to lengthy appendices; the main text sometimes asserts results (e.g., "our work requires fewer and more interpretable order parameters") without sufficient elaboration for a reader to independently verify the comparative claim against cited competing theories.

The extension to committee machines/nonlinear models (Section J) is left essentially as an unsolved setup with no results, so the paper's applicability beyond linear/kernel regression remains speculative despite framing this as future relevance to real networks.

strengths: The paper derives a rigorous dynamical mean-field theory (via MSRDJ formalism + variational Gaussian approximation) that unifies several previously separate frameworks for studying generalization in random feature/kernel regression: static Bayesian GP inference (Canatar et al.), gradient flow with/without weight decay (Advani et al.), and stochastic Langevin dynamics. This unification is non-trivial and technically well executed.

The theory yields a compact and interpretable description: only two self-averaging order parameters (a collective response function and an autocorrelation function) fully characterize the high-dimensional dynamics, which is claimed to be simpler than the auxiliary-field constructions used in closely related prior work (e.g., Bordelon et al. 2024).

Analytical predictions (mean discrepancy dynamics, bias-variance decomposition of the test error, neural scaling law exponents, and a closed-form optimal early-stopping time t* = (β/2)(α/(1+α)) that is independent of P and N) are clean, interpretable, and directly tied to the power-law kernel spectrum.

Extensive numerical validation: theory curves are compared against simulations across multiple figures (Figs. 1–5) with good quantitative agreement, including for varying noise temperature, regularization strength, and sample size, lending credibility to the derivation.

The paper explicitly reduces to known results in limiting cases (recovers Canatar et al. 2021 in the noiseless stationary limit, and Bordelon et al. 2024 in the P,t→∞ regime), which is a strong internal consistency check and situates the contribution clearly within existing literature.
Extensions to label noise (Appendix H) and a sketch for committee machines (Appendix J) demonstrate the flexibility of the underlying formalism beyond the base linear/GP setting.

The appendices provide a very complete and transparent derivation (identification of order parameters, careful treatment of self-averaging terms, VGA justification via CLT), which aids reproducibility of the theoretical results.
weaknesses: All experiments are on synthetic Gaussian random features with imposed power-law eigenvalue spectra; no experiments on real data or real trained networks are provided to demonstrate that the theory's qualitative/quantitative predictions carry over beyond the idealized linear/GP setting.

The committee machine extension (Appendix J) is incomplete — the disorder average is explicitly "left for future work," so this section reads more as a promissory remark than a validated contribution, and its inclusion may overstate the paper's scope of applicability to non-linear networks.

The presentation is very dense and physics-notation-heavy (MSRDJ formalism, replica-like manipulations, Wishart cumulant expansions), which may limit accessibility to a broad ICML audience without significant background in statistical field theory; a higher-level summary of the key mechanistic insights earlier in the paper would help.

Finite-size (N) effects are visible and non-negligible in the numerics (e.g., Fig. 4's N^{-α} correction term is described as 'cannot be neglected'), yet the discussion of when the asymptotic theory is quantitatively reliable in practice is somewhat brief.

The core assumptions (Gaussian i.i.d. features per sample, exact orthogonality/diagonal covariance structure, noiseless teacher as default) are fairly restrictive relative to real feature/kernel spectra from trained networks, and the paper does not empirically probe robustness to violations of these assumptions (e.g., correlated features, non-Gaussian noise).

Related work comparisons, while present, could more explicitly quantify what new predictions or insights this framework offers beyond prior dynamical models (e.g., Bordelon et al. 2024, Paquette et al.) in terms of testable, novel phenomena rather than reformulation/simplification of known regimes.
